# Ephesians 6: notes for the commentary

**How to read these notes.** I ran out of research tools before I could cover everything. Several sources I didn't reach: Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Anglican, Assemblies of God (ag.org), bibleodyssey.org, the NET Bible notes, Catholic.com, OCA, and anything on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. They are left out below. Three pages I read in full (Guzik's Enduring Word, Wesley's Notes and Chrysostom's Homily 21) are summarised with their URL and no citation tags.

---

## Part A: Family and household (vv. 1–9)

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the command also gives parents a job: they have to *teach* obedience. Obeying "in the Lord" makes it part of the child's Christian obedience. He adds that grown children owe their parents honour, not obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley reads it as obedience "in all things lawful," done for the Lord's sake. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Ellicott says "in the Lord" puts the relationship within the unity binding all to Christ, in virtue of which the parental authority and the right freedom of the child are both hallowed. Benson adds that this includes your unbelieving parents, in every thing consistent with your duty to the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6.htm
- Ligonier (Reformed) says Paul is mainly speaking to children who still live at home. Adult children can draw principles from the verse. Abusive, neglectful, and impenitently foolish parents are not to be honored in the same way as good parents. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/obeying-parents-in-the-lord
- A note quoted in the CCEL Chrysostom edition (Braune) says that addressing children in a letter to the church presupposes that the Apostle regards them as belonging to the Church, present at public worship. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf113/npnf113.iii.iv.xxii.html
- *Orthodox/Catholic (Church Fathers):* Chrysostom takes "in the Lord" to mean "according to the Lord," that is, wherever obeying would not offend God. If a pagan or heretic father commands what is against God, the child should not obey. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230121.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik notes that Paul is quoting Deuteronomy 5:16. Christians usually split the Ten Commandments 4/6, but Jews split them 5/5. That puts honouring parents on the duty-to-God side. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley defines "honour" as love, reverence, obedience and help. He thinks the mother is named because she is more easily slighted. He calls this the first commandment with a promise because the promise in the second commandment covers the whole law, not that command alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Chrysostom says "first" refers to the promise, not to rank. Parents are, after God, the authors of our being. Someone who doesn't honour them will not be gentle with strangers either. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230121.htm

**v. 3**
- Wesley says long life usually comes to very dutiful children. In the Christian era, though, he reads the promise mainly in a higher, spiritual sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Guzik quotes Foulkes: when respect for parents fails, a community decays and will not "live long." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Chrysostom says Paul promises young listeners long life, not the kingdom, because that is what children can grasp. He then urges parents to care more about endless life hereafter than about long life here. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230121.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik says provoking means an unkind, over-critical manner. He quotes Wood: in a culture where the father had absolute authority, considering the child's feelings was revolutionary. He quotes Lloyd-Jones: a parent must control himself before disciplining. Fathers can't hand this job to mothers or Sunday school. "Training" means corrective discipline (the same word as Heb 12) and "admonition" means teaching. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley says mothers are included, but fathers are named because they tend to be sterner. Children should be raised "with all tenderness and mildness." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Chrysostom gives examples of provoking: disinheriting children, or treating them like slaves rather than free persons. He pleads for Scripture reading from the earliest age. That isn't "the business of monks," he says; the aim is to make the child a Christian. He points to Hannah and to teaching children to despise riches. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230121.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik says "as to Christ" changes how we see work. He quotes Moule: the gospel's plan was "not to batter, but to undermine" slavery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Ellicott says the institution is left alone, but a shared fellowship in Christ enunciates a principle absolutely incompatible with slavery, and destined to destroy it. To him the slave is a man in spiritual and immortal being, not a "living tool" or "chattel". https://biblehub.com/ephesians/6-5.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says that however unjust their position, Paul counselled obedience this course being the best for ultimately working out their emancipation. Benson says such masters have the command of your bodies, but not of your souls and consciences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6-5.htm
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org) takes "fear and trembling" as a deep sense of humility, and of dependence on God. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-submission-and-slavery-ephesians-65-9
- Ligonier applies the passage today as a principle: we serve our earthly supervisors with an eye to the Lord. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/serving-earthly-masters
- Background: a Bible Hub article identifies Ephesians 5:21–6:9 as a "household code," a form common in Greco-Roman moral philosophy. It says Paul reshapes the form so that every command is "in the Lord" and runs both ways. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Eph_6_5_tell_slaves_to_obey.htm

**v. 6**
- Wesley defines "eye-service" as working better when watched than at other times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Deffinbaugh: The Ephesians were not instructed to obey their masters and Christ, but to obey their masters in obedience to Christ. The fundamental obedience is therefore not to masters, but to the Master. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-submission-and-slavery-ephesians-65-9

**v. 7**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: grace lets us do heaven's business while we attend to earth's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley speaks of "making every action of common life a sacrifice to God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Barnes says a Christian can serve Christ as a servant as acceptably serve the Lord Jesus in the condition of a servant, as if he were a minister of the gospel, or a king on a throne. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6-5.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik says God won't let hard work go unrewarded. He warns of a common cycle: conversion leads to diligence, diligence to prosperity, prosperity to drifting, and then to discipline. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Deffinbaugh says the Christian slave learns to look for reward from the heavenly Master, not the earthly one, and to wait for that day. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-submission-and-slavery-ephesians-65-9

**v. 9**
- Guzik quotes Moule on the "equal obligation" of slave and owner, with "no word of Revolution." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Deffinbaugh: In the world, there is a double standard, one for masters, and another for slaves. But with God there is one standard. The one specific command to masters is to give up threatening. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-submission-and-slavery-ephesians-65-9
- Matthew Henry: You have a Master to obey, and you and they are but fellow-servants in respect to Christ Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6-5.htm

---

## Part B: The armour of God (vv. 10–20)

**v. 10**
- Guzik says it literally means "strengthen yourselves in the Lord," probably echoing David in 1 Samuel 30:6. "Might" is the reserve of strength and "power" is that strength at work. He includes Lloyd-Jones's list of things that drain a Christian's strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley notes that "brethren" appears only here in the letter, a word soldiers use with each other in the field. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Gann says "finally" probably means "what remains for me say to you." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/6-10.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik says the armour is God's in two senses. It comes from him, and it *is His actual armor*. In the Old Testament, it is the LORD who wears the armor (Isaiah 59:17). He now shares that armor with us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Gill disagrees: it is Not that which God himself is sometimes clothed with, and uses against his enemies; but what he has provided for his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6-11.htm
- JFB: the image comes from Roman armour, with Paul in Rome. The Ephesians were familiar with the idea of the gods giving armor to mythical heroes. Putting on the armour also means putting on Christ (Rom 13:14). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_006.cfm
- Precept Austin notes there is no armour for the back. It says "stand against" is a military phrase meaning to stand in front of with a view to holding a critical position, to hold one's ground. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_611

**v. 12**
- Guzik says Paul isn't calling believers to *enter* spiritual warfare; he states it as a fact. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley guesses that the principalities stay mostly in the "citadel" of darkness, while other spirits are given "the provinces of the world." He says these spirits stir up unbelief, pride, envy and hatred. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Chuck Smith says the powers are spirit entities; they are captains and lieutenants of the demon ranks. They are called principalities, powers, authorities, dominions, and they have various rankings of evil spirits. Constable notes that Stott refuted the view that the principalities and powers are only structures of thought, especially embodied in the state and its institutions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/6-12.html
- Clarke records another reading: some translate the phrase "about heavenly things," meaning we fight these spirits over the heavenly things promised to us. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/ephesians/6-12.html
- *Debated modern teaching: "territorial spirits."* Piper (Baptist) describes Peter Wagner's teaching that the church is called to fight evil spirits that attach themselves to specific territories, regimes or institutions, citing Eph 6:12. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/angels-and-prayer
- GotQuestions lists Eph 6:12 among the verses behind the idea. It says believers taking it as their duty to engage territorial demons cannot be justified by Scripture. https://www.gotquestions.org/territorial-spirits.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik says Paul's emphasis in vv. 11 and 13 is to *stand* when Satan attacks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley says the war never stops, but some days are worse than others. The "evil day" may be the approach of death or a trial during life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Precept Austin says Paul does not say for us to hunt down or to actively pursue our spiritual enemies, but to stand firm. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_613

**v. 14**
- Guzik divides the armour into pieces to *have* all the time (belt, breastplate, boots) and pieces to *take up* in battle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- Wesley says "truth" means both gospel truths and "truth in the inward parts." The breastplate is the righteousness in which Christ will present us faultless through his blood, and it guards the conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- John Brown pictures the soldier first tucking up his garments, and says It is God's truth = His Word = that keeps us from tripping and falling! https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/brown_john/Eph/Eph_6v_10-24.cfm

**v. 15**
- Wesley says this footwear is needed for the long journey and race of life. It works as the peace and love of God ruling in the heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html

**v. 16**
- Guzik says "above all" really means "in addition to the previous," and it applies to each of the three pieces of armor that follow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- JFB prefers "over all," a shield covering everything else, and notes that Alford reads "besides all." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_006.cfm
- Wesley takes the fiery darts to be furious temptations and "sudden injections of the devil." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html

**v. 17**
- Wesley says the helmet is the *hope* of salvation (1 Thess 5:8), ranging from confidence that God will finish his work in us up to full assurance. The sword is the only attacking weapon so far. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Guzik says the Spirit supplies the sword and helps us use it. We must not treat the Bible as a book of magic charms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/
- JFB says Christ's use of Scripture in his temptation is our pattern. It counts prayer as a second attacking weapon, a "spear." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_006.cfm

**v. 18: the main point of disagreement (does "pray in the Spirit" mean tongues?)**
- *Traditional reading:* Barnes says it means praying by the Holy Spirit's help rather than a heartfelt human spirit, and The former idea seems, however, to be the correct one. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/ephesians/6-18.html
- Older interpreters such as Erasmus and Grotius read it as the human spirit, meaning heartfelt prayer. Expositor's says it is "in the Holy Spirit," the sphere or element in which alone true prayer of all different kinds can proceed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6-18.htm
- *Methodist:* Wesley says it means "through the influence of the Holy Spirit" and covers every kind of prayer (public, private, silent, spoken). He warns against those who use only silent prayer. He suggests we get few answers because we intercede too little for others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- *Baptist:* Piper says it isn't tongues, because the verse says "at all times." All of our praying is to be in the Spirit, not just one part of our praying — like praying in tongues. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-we-pray-in-the-spirit
- *Evangelical:* GotQuestions notes that Some, based on 1 Corinthians 14:15, equate praying in the Spirit with praying in tongues. It concludes the phrase means praying in the power of the Spirit, by the leading of the Spirit, and according to His will, not as praying in tongues. https://www.gotquestions.org/praying-Spirit.html Precept Austin takes the same view. https://www.preceptaustin.org/praying_in_the_spirit
- *Charismatic-leaning (Calvary Chapel):* Chuck Smith asks "What is it to pray in the Spirit?" and answers with Romans 8 and the tongues verses of 1 Corinthians 14:2, 14–15. His notes list these texts without stating a conclusion. He also sees prayer as the move through prayer that we begin to attack the enemy, and his strongholds. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Eph/Eph_77.cfm
- I found no Pentecostal denominational source (such as ag.org) arguing the tongues reading directly.
- Guzik says prayer is what puts the armour to work: the prayerless Christian can be strong and wearing all the armor; but never accomplishes anything. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/

**v. 19**
- Wesley takes "opening my mouth" to mean God removing every inner and outer hindrance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Guzik applies vv. 18–19 to praying for missionaries (the title of a video on the page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-6/

**v. 20**
- Wesley contrasts the pomp of human ambassadors with Christ's ambassador in chains. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
- Ellicott links the armour image to Paul writing in the watchful presence of the full-armed Roman "soldiers that kept" St. Paul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/6.htm

---

## Part C: Closing (vv. 21–24)

**vv. 21–22**
- Wesley reads "ye also" as "as well as others." Tychicus would encourage them by telling of the help Paul found from God and of the gospel's progress. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html

**v. 23**
- Wesley says this verse sums up the whole letter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html

**v. 24**
- Wesley notes "in sincerity" can mean "in incorruption." He reads it as loving Christ without corrupting his gospel or mixing in corrupt affections, and continuing until grace becomes glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-6.html
